{{Short description|Mathematical operator}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Skorokhod integral''', also named '''Hitsuda–Skorokhod integral''', often denoted <math>\delta</math>, is an [[Operator (mathematics)|operator]] of great importance in the theory of [[stochastic processes]].  It is named after the [[Ukraine|Ukrainian]] [[mathematician]] [[Anatoliy Skorokhod]] and [[Japan]]ese mathematician [[Masuyuki Hitsuda]].  Part of its importance is that it unifies several concepts:
* <math>\delta</math> is an extension of the [[Itô integral]] to non-[[adapted process]]es;
* <math>\delta</math> is the [[adjoint operator|adjoint]] of the [[Malliavin derivative]], which is fundamental to the stochastic [[calculus of variations]] ([[Malliavin calculus]]);
* <math>\delta</math> is an infinite-dimensional generalization of the [[divergence]] operator from classical [[vector calculus]].

The integral was introduced by Hitsuda in 1972<ref>{{cite journal|first=Masuyuki|last=Hitsuda|title=Formula for Brownian partial derivatives|journal=Second Japan-USSR Symp. Probab. Th.2.|date=1972|pages=111–114}}</ref> and by Skorokhod in 1975.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Kuo|first=Hui-Hsiung|date=2014|title=The Itô calculus and white noise theory: a brief survey toward general stochastic integration|journal=Communications on Stochastic Analysis|volume=8|number=1|doi=10.31390/cosa.8.1.07|url=https://repository.lsu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1325&context=cosa|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Definition==

===Preliminaries: the Malliavin derivative===

Consider a fixed [[probability space]] <math>(\Omega, \Sigma, \mathbf{P})</math> and a [[Hilbert space]] <math>H</math>; <math>\mathbf{E}</math> denotes [[expected value|expectation]] with respect to <math>\mathbf{P}</math>

<math display="block">\mathbf{E} [X] := \int_\Omega X(\omega) \, \mathrm{d} \mathbf{P}(\omega).</math>

Intuitively speaking, the Malliavin derivative of a random variable <math>F</math> in <math>L^p(\Omega)</math> is defined by expanding it in terms of Gaussian random variables that are parametrized by the elements of <math>H</math> and differentiating the expansion formally; the Skorokhod integral is the adjoint operation to the Malliavin derivative.

Consider a family of <math>\mathbb{R}</math>-valued [[random variables]] <math>W(h)</math>, indexed by the elements <math>h</math> of the Hilbert space <math>H</math>.  Assume further that each <math>W(h)</math> is a Gaussian ([[normal distribution|normal]]) random variable, that the map taking <math>h</math> to <math>W(h)</math> is a [[linear map]], and that the [[expected value|mean]] and [[covariance]] structure is given by

<math display="block">\mathbf{E} [W(h)] = 0,</math>
<math display="block">\mathbf{E} [W(g) W(h)] = \langle g, h \rangle_H,</math>

for all <math>g</math> and <math>h</math> in <math>H</math>.  It can be shown that, given <math>H</math>, there always exists a probability space <math>(\Omega, \Sigma, \mathbf{P})</math> and a family of random variables with the above properties.  The Malliavin derivative is essentially defined by formally setting the derivative of the random variable <math>W(h)</math> to be <math>h</math>, and then extending this definition to "[[smooth function|smooth enough]]" random variables.  For a random variable <math>F</math> of the form

<math display="block">F = f(W(h_1), \ldots, W(h_n)),</math>

where <math>f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}</math> is smooth, the '''Malliavin derivative''' is defined using the earlier "formal definition" and the chain rule:

<math display="block">\mathrm{D} F := \sum_{i = 1}^n \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} (W(h_1), \ldots, W(h_n)) h_i.</math>

In other words, whereas <math>F</math> was a real-valued random variable, its derivative <math>\mathrm{D}F</math> is an <math>H</math>-valued random variable, an element of the space <math>L^p(\Omega; H)</math>.  Of course, this procedure only defines <math>\mathrm{D}F</math> for "smooth" random variables, but an approximation procedure can be employed to define <math>\mathrm{D}F</math> for <math>F</math> in a large subspace of <math>L^p(\Omega)</math>;  the [[domain of a function|domain]] of <math>\mathrm{D}</math> is the [[closure (topology)|closure]] of the smooth random variables in the [[seminorm]] :

<math display="block">\| F \|_{1, p} := \big( \mathbf{E}[|F|^p] + \mathbf{E}[\| \mathrm{D}F \|_H^p] \big)^{1/p}.</math>

This space is denoted by <math>\mathbf{D}^{1, p}</math> and is called the [[Watanabe–Sobolev space]].

===The Skorokhod integral===

For simplicity, consider now just the case <math>p = 2</math>.  The '''Skorokhod integral''' <math>\delta</math> is defined to be the <math>L^2</math>-adjoint of the Malliavin derivative <math>\mathrm{D}</math>.  Just as <math>\mathrm{D}</math> was not defined on the whole of <math>L^2(\Omega)</math>, <math>\delta</math> is not defined on the whole of <math>L^2(\Omega; H)</math>:  the domain of <math>\delta</math> consists of those processes <math>u</math> in <math>L^2(\Omega; H)</math> for which there exists a constant <math>C(u)</math> such that, for all <math>F</math> in <math>\mathbf{D}^{1, 2}</math>,

<math display="block">\big| \mathbf{E} [ \langle \mathrm{D} F, u \rangle_{H} ] \big| \leq C(u) \| F \|_{L^{2} (\Omega)}.</math>

The '''Skorokhod integral''' of a process <math>u</math> in <math>L^2(\Omega; H)</math> is a real-valued random variable <math>\delta u</math> in <math>L^2(\Omega)</math>; if <math>u</math> lies in the domain of <math>\delta</math>, then <math>\delta u</math> is defined by the relation that, for all <math>F \in \mathbf{D}^{1, 2}</math>,

<math display="block">\mathbf{E} [F \, \delta u] = \mathbf{E} [ \langle \mathrm{D}F, u \rangle_{H} ].</math>

Just as the Malliavin derivative <math>\mathrm{D}</math> was first defined on simple, smooth random variables, the Skorokhod integral has a simple expression for "simple processes":  if <math>u</math> is given by

<math display="block">u = \sum_{j = 1}^{n} F_{j} h_{j}</math>

with <math>F_j</math> smooth and <math>h_j</math> in <math>H</math>, then

<math display="block">\delta u = \sum_{j = 1}^{n} \left( F_{j} W(h_{j}) - \langle \mathrm{D} F_{j}, h_{j} \rangle_{H} \right).</math>

==Properties==

* The [[isometry]] property:  for any process <math>u</math> in <math>\mathbf{D}^{1, p}</math> that lies in the domain of <math>\delta</math>, <math display="block">\mathbf{E} \big[ (\delta u)^{2} \big] = \mathbf{E} \int | u_t |^{2} dt + \mathbf{E} \int D_s u_t\, D_t u_s\,ds\, dt.</math> If <math>u</math> is an adapted process, then <math>D_s u_t = 0</math> for <math>s > t</math>, so the second term on the right-hand side vanishes. The Skorokhod and Itô integrals coincide in that case, and the above equation becomes the [[Itô isometry]].
* The derivative of a Skorokhod integral is given by the formula <math display="block">\mathrm{D}_{h} (\delta u) = \langle u, h \rangle_{H} + \delta (\mathrm{D}_{h} u),</math> where <math>\mathrm{D}_h X</math> stands for <math>(\mathrm{D}X)(h)</math>, the random variable that is the value of the process <math>\mathrm{D} X</math> at "time" <math>h</math> in <math>H</math>.
* The Skorokhod integral of the product of a random variable <math>F</math> in <math>\mathbf{D}^{1, 2}</math> and a process <math>u</math> in <math> \operatorname{dom}(\delta)</math> is given by the formula <math display="block">\delta (F u) = F \, \delta u - \langle \mathrm{D} F, u \rangle_{H}.</math>

== Alternatives ==
An alternative to the Skorokhod integral is the [[Ogawa integral]].
